items.caption:
Stripe CEO Patrick Collison says the number of new businesses starting on Stripe is up around 2x year over year.

He calls it the largest relative jump they have seen, and says it isn't just more lightweight projects: the median new business is doing better than a year ago, and time to revenue for Atlas companies is falling.

Is this the best time ever to start a company, or just the easiest?

Source: Y Combinator, Patrick Collison: Is AI Breaking the Lean Startup Playbook? Full video: youtube.com/watch?v=5d6y3poKwK4

Stripe CEO Patrick Collison says many of the most successful companies of the last 10 years are very anti-lean startup.

He names the AI labs and Anduril, and argues that with today's capital and AI, founders can start much more aggressive and ambitious things up front instead of testing tiny versions first.

Is "start small and iterate" still good advice in 2026?

items.caption:
Paul Graham says what actually motivates founders day to day is the fear of failure.

The chance of getting rich matters, but in the moment it's the fear of disaster or looking like a fool: when your server is crashing, you're not thinking about becoming a billionaire, you just don't want your model train set to break.

Founders: is fear your fuel, or something you had to learn to switch off?

Source: Y Combinator, Paul Graham On Startups, Ambition, and Great Founders. Full video: youtube.com/watch?v=5bxp78i96S8

items.caption:
Paul Graham says that with startups, there's no easy major.

Early in YC's history, people started applying for the prestige, like applying to Harvard. But Harvard lets you slide through an easy major; a startup is like being forced to study theoretical physics, and he calls it a really unsuitable credential.

Would you start a company for the credential, or only for the problem?
